one_liner: Branchless in-place unstable C quicksort/quadsort hybrid, ~1.4-1.5x faster than pdqsort on random 32/64-bit ints.
what_it_does: crumsort is an in-place, unstable, adaptive sort for C arrays that partitions like quicksort but falls back to quadsort for small partitions and pathological cases. It exposes the standard qsort(array, nmemb, size, cmp) signature plus a crumsort_prim(array, nmemb, size) entry point for 32/64-bit primitive integers that skips the comparison function. Custom types are supported the normal qsort way, via pointers and a comparator.
how_it_is_fast: Its 'fulcrum' partitioning scheme (a BlockQuicksort-style branchless variant of Hoare partitioning) holds the pivot in a swap slot so each element move takes 2 assignments instead of 3, and widens the swap buffer to batch 16 boundless comparisons branchlessly. Pivot selection scales pseudomedian-of-9/median-of-16 for small partitions up to median-of-128/256/512 for large ones. An analyzer pre-scans for sortedness and reverts to quadsort per segment, and quadsort (not insertion sort) handles partitions under 24 elements. Pivot retention (borrowed from pdqsort) triggers a reverse partition on runs of duplicate pivots for generic/low-cardinality data.
when_to_use: Sorting large arrays (README cites >1,000,000 elements) of random-order 32/64-bit integers or pointer-sized keys where stability is not required
Sorting 'tables' (structs/rows) by a 64-bit key or pointer, including tables that embed long doubles, since crumsort only moves the pointer, not the 128-bit payload
Data with many duplicate/low-cardinality values (e.g. gender, age columns) thanks to the dual-pivot-style reverse partition on repeated pivots
Environments where you can vendor plain C source (no package manager) and want a qsort drop-in with better throughput on primitives
Throughput-oriented batch sorts rather than latency-sensitive incremental/partial sorts
when_not_to_use: Sorting arrays of long double (128-bit) directly as the array element type — README and this session's benchmark both show pdqsort winning there (0.005975s vs 0.008316s avg, 100K elements)
Any workload requiring stability (equal keys must keep relative order) — crumsort is explicitly unstable; use fluxsort or quadsort instead

Large nearly-sorted arrays where fluxsort will outperform it — crumsort runs on only 512 elements of auxiliary stack memory and, being unstable, scrambles pre-existing order more than fluxsort's mid-partition ordered-run detection
Projects wanting an actively maintained dependency — last commit 2024-07-27, tagged stale, and the author's own TODO admits the long-double slowdown is unfixed

Codebases wanting a single, normally-linked translation unit — crumsort.h uses macro-based generic instantiation that re-#includes crumsort.c per type, which is source-drop only, not a conventional compiled library

integration.dependencies: none (crumsort.h pulls in quadsort.h/quadsort.c from the same repo; both are vendored together)
integration.min_toolchain: C11 (crumsort.h includes stdalign.h); README's own benchmark compiles it with g++ -O3 -w -fpermissive, so it also compiles as permissive C++
integration.platforms: not restricted to any ISA in source — plain portable C with no explicit SIMD intrinsics (branchlessness relies on compiler codegen, not intrinsics); README benchmark run was WSL/x86-64 only, no other platform is documented
integration.thread_safety: not documented; no internal global/static mutable state was found in crumsort.c, so concurrent sorts of separate arrays look safe, but this is not stated by the author
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — qsort-API-compatible (same call shape as C's qsort), not std::sort's iterator/comparator interface, and it is unstable so it cannot substitute for std::stable_sort

gotchas: Header/source layering is macro-driven: crumsort.h does #define VAR/FUNC then #include "crumsort.c" repeatedly to generate typed variants — you vendor and #include the .c files, you don't link a normal compiled object

crumsort_prim() only covers 32/64-bit signed/unsigned integers (size must be sizeof(int)/sizeof(long long), +1 for unsigned per an internal assert); other primitive/custom types require editing crumsort.h/quadsort.h yourself
Uses 512 elements of stack swap memory shared with quadsort, plus O(log n) recursion stack — not a strictly O(1)-memory sort despite being 'in-place' in the informal sense
The `cmp` macro must be defined (uncommented, per README) to get the fully branchless comparison path; without it you fall back to a normal function-pointer comparator with lower throughput
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Over fluxsort (same author, catalogued sibling): pick crumsort when you don't need stability and want the extra throughput crumsort gets from being truly in-place, especially sorting large random-order integer/pointer arrays or tables with long-double payloads — fluxsort remains the better choice for large near-sorted data or when stability matters. crumsort is not shown against BlockQuicksort, Boost.Sort spreadsort, or IPS⁴o in this repo, so no direct comparison to those siblings is documented.
verified_claims_summary: Author's own wolfsort/bench.c harness (g++ -O3 -w -fpermissive, WSL gcc 7.5.0 on Ubuntu 18.04, no CPU model given) shows crumsort averaging 0.001927s vs pdqsort's 0.002668s on 100,000 random 64-bit ints (~1.4x) and 0.001812s vs 0.002705s on 32-bit ints (~1.5x), each best-of/avg-of 100 runs; on 128-bit long doubles pdqsort is faster (0.005975s vs crumsort's 0.008316s). No comparison against std::sort or std::stable_sort appears on the page.
status_note: Maintenance is stale (last commit 2024-07-27) but the Unlicense public-domain dedication and small source-drop footprint (two headers, two .c files) make it cheap to vendor and freeze at a known-good revision regardless.
